messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 61

He is thirty years old, a carpenter who has spent most of his adult life working with his hands, and he talks about wood the way some people talk about weather or prayer. Before everything changed, he liked the predictability of his days: the smell of sawdust in the morning, the rhythm of measuring twice and cutting once, the quiet satisfaction of fitting one thing cleanly to another. He is married, and when he describes that earlier period of his life, he does so in practical terms. He was working hard, coming home tired, saving for a bigger house, thinking in the ordinary way about the future.

The event he returns to begins on a job site late in the afternoon. He and a small crew are framing the second story of a residential build. He remembers the angle of the sun, the dry chill in the air, the way everyone was eager to finish one last section before packing up. A younger coworker, someone he had worked beside for months, is up on the scaffolding helping guide a beam into place. He hears a shout first, sharp and wrong, then the metallic clatter of something slipping. When he looks up, he sees the man lose footing and go over the side. He still describes that moment as if it happens in pieces: the body twisting, the useless reach for the rail, the sound of impact, and then a strange silence before everyone starts moving.

He is the first one to reach him. He kneels in gravel and mud, yelling his coworker’s name, seeing blood where blood should not be, trying to remember what to do with his hands. He calls 911, presses where someone tells him to press, hears himself talking too loudly, hears another part of himself noticing absurd details—the torn seam of a work jacket, a hammer lying a few feet away, the smell of wet plywood. The paramedics arrive quickly, but in his memory it is endless. His coworker dies before the ambulance leaves.

In the first few weeks afterward, he tells himself he is doing what a man is supposed to do. He gives a statement, goes back to work, accepts the casseroles and handshakes and the repeated assurances that it was an accident. But he starts waking in the middle of the night already sitting up, heart pounding, his T-shirt damp with sweat. Sometimes he sees the fall before he is fully awake; sometimes he hears the sound. His wife reaches for him and he jerks away before he realizes where he is. He becomes embarrassed by how quickly his body reacts, as if he is failing some private test.

On site, he begins to notice everything that could go wrong. He scans ladders, harnesses, guardrails, bolts. If someone climbs without clipping in, his chest tightens and his jaw locks. The noise of dropped metal sends a shock through him so strong that he has to stop what he is doing. He avoids the upper levels whenever he can, making excuses to stay on the ground cutting studs or organizing tools. He tells people he is just being careful, but he knows the truth is narrower than that. He cannot bear the sight of a man near an edge.

His wife says he is there and not there. At dinner he loses track of the conversation when his mind drifts back to the gravel and blood. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks the locks twice before bed, then again after brushing his teeth. When his phone rings unexpectedly, irritation flashes across his face before he answers. Small frustrations that used to pass now ignite him. He snaps when traffic stalls, when dishes clatter, when a neighbor’s teenage son climbs onto a roof to clean gutters. Almost immediately he feels ashamed.

He has stopped driving past the road that leads to that house. If a job comes in near that neighborhood, he trades with someone else. He no longer watches the news because footage of accidents, ambulances, or anything falling makes his stomach drop. His wife once suggests they attend a memorial barbecue held by the dead coworker’s family, and he says no so quickly that she falls silent. Later, alone in the garage, he cries with an anger that feels aimed everywhere.

What troubles him most is not only the memory itself but what it has done to his sense of himself. He used to think of himself as solid, useful, steady in a crisis. Now he second-guesses everything. He replays the timing of that afternoon while cutting trim, while showering, while lying beside his wife in the dark. If he had looked up sooner, yelled louder, checked the scaffold himself, insisted on stopping earlier—his mind builds these alternate versions over and over, though none of them bring relief.

Months have passed, but his world remains organized around the fall. He sleeps lightly, works tensely, and moves through each day as if danger is waiting just above eye level. Even on calmer evenings, when he is home with his wife and the house is quiet, part of him stays braced, listening for the sound of something giving way.
